sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 107 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Let the redeemed of the LORD say so
study.intro: Psalm 107 opens Book V of the Psalter with a call for the redeemed to give thanks. It paints four pictures of people in trouble: lost travelers, prisoners in chains, the sick near death, and sailors in a storm. Each group cries out, God rescues, and they are urged to thank Him. The psalm ends by showing how God overturns human fortunes, and calls the wise to consider His loving devotion.
study.context: Psalm 107 follows directly from Psalm 106, which ended with the prayer 'gather us from the nations.' Psalm 107 answers that the LORD has gathered the redeemed from east and west, north and south. Its four scenes share a repeated pattern: trouble, a cry to the LORD, rescue, and a call to give thanks. The refrains make it easy to sing and remember, and the closing verses read like wisdom teaching.
study.peopleNote: No author is named. The people in the psalm are unnamed groups: wanderers, prisoners, the sick and sailors. God is never portrayed as a human figure in planned art; His rescue is shown through paths, opened doors, calm water and restored people.

verses.title: Good and enduring love
verses.heading: Give thanks, for He is good
verses.meaning: The psalm opens, 'Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.' It is the same line that began Psalm 106, but now it introduces stories of rescue rather than confession. Everything that follows will illustrate this sentence. Each group of people in trouble discovers in their own way that God is good and that His covenant love does not run out.
verses.context: This refrain appears in Psalm 106:1, 118:1 and as the repeated line of Psalm 136. Ezra 3:11 records the people singing it when the foundation of the second temple was laid, a fitting echo for a psalm about the return of the scattered.
explore: Good
Morally perfect and generous; God's goodness is both His character and His kindness toward us.
Endures forever
Continues without end, never wearing out or being withdrawn over time.
verses.reflect: Which part of your own story shows you that God is good?
verses.alt: Returning travelers singing together on a road at sunrise.

verses.title: Let the redeemed speak
verses.heading: Redeemed from the hand of the enemy
verses.meaning: Verse 2 says, 'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy.' Those who have been rescued are told to speak up. Thanksgiving is not only felt; it is said aloud. The redeemed are people bought back from captivity, and their voices are the best witness that God still saves.
verses.context: Isaiah 62:12 calls God's restored people 'the Redeemed of the LORD.' Isaiah 35:10 pictures the redeemed returning to Zion with singing. Revelation 12:11 says believers overcame by the word of their testimony.
explore: Redeemed
Bought back or set free at a price, like a relative paying to release a family member.
Say so
To speak out openly, giving testimony to what God has done for you.
verses.reflect: When did you last tell someone out loud what God has done for you?
verses.alt: A man telling his story to neighbors gathered at a village well.

verses.title: Gathered from every direction
verses.heading: From east and west, north and south
verses.meaning: Verse 3 adds that God 'gathered them from the lands, from east and west, from north and south.' The prayer at the end of Psalm 106 has been answered. Scattered people have been brought home from every compass point. No one is too far away for God to bring back. For a people who had prayed in exile, this line was the proof that God had heard them.
verses.context: Psalm 106:47 prayed, 'gather us from the nations.' Isaiah 43:5-6 promises God will gather His people from east, west, north and south. Jesus says in Matthew 8:11 that many will come from east and west to the feast of the kingdom.
explore: Gathered
Brought together from scattered places into one people and one home.
East and west
A way of saying every direction, so that no one is left out or forgotten.
verses.reflect: Who do you know who feels too far away to come home to God?
verses.alt: Caravans approaching a hilltop city from several roads at once.

verses.title: Lost in the wastelands
verses.heading: No path to a city
verses.meaning: Verse 4 begins the first scene: 'Some wandered in desert wastelands, finding no path to a city in which to dwell.' These are travelers who have lost their way. Without a road, there is no shelter, no water, no community. The picture fits anyone who feels lost in life, without direction or a place to belong.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 8:15 describes the vast and dreadful wilderness Israel crossed. Hebrews 11:13-16 speaks of God's people as strangers seeking a homeland and a city God has prepared. Isaiah 49:10 promises God will guide them to springs of water.
explore: Wastelands
Empty, barren land with no water, food or safe places to stay.
City in which to dwell
A settled home with safety, neighbors and provision for life.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel lost or without a settled place right now?
verses.alt: Travelers in head cloths searching across endless dunes for a trail.

verses.title: Fainting souls
verses.heading: Hungry and thirsty
verses.meaning: Verse 5 says, 'They were hungry and thirsty; their soul fainted within them.' Their bodies were failing, and so was their spirit. The word 'soul' here means their whole life. Long wandering wears down more than the body; it drains hope until a person feels ready to give up. Hunger and thirst here point beyond the body to a longing only God can meet.
verses.context: Psalm 63:1 describes a soul that thirsts for God in a dry and weary land. Lamentations 2:12 tells of children fainting from hunger. Jesus says in John 6:35 that whoever comes to Him will never hunger or thirst.
explore: Soul
The whole living person, body and inner life together, not just a spirit.
Fainted
Grew weak and faint, near collapse from exhaustion or lack of strength.
verses.reflect: What has been draining your strength and hope lately?
verses.alt: An exhausted traveler resting against a rock in the desert heat.

verses.title: The wanderers cry out
verses.heading: He delivered them from distress
verses.meaning: Verse 6 gives the first refrain: 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He delivered them from their distress.' The turning point is a simple cry. The wanderers did not find the road by their own skill. They called to God, and He answered. This refrain will return four times, showing that every kind of trouble has the same remedy.
verses.context: Exodus 3:7 says God heard Israel's cry in Egypt. Psalm 34:6 says, 'This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him.' Romans 10:13 promises that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
explore: Cried out
Called urgently for help, often aloud, from a place of need.
Distress
Pressing trouble or anguish that squeezes a person on every side.
verses.reflect: What keeps you from crying out to God sooner when you are in trouble?
verses.alt: A traveler on his knees in the sand, face lifted toward the sky.

verses.title: A straight path
verses.heading: Led to a city to live in
verses.meaning: Verse 7 says, 'He led them on a straight path to reach a city where they could live.' God did not only rescue them from the desert; He guided them to a home. The path was straight, not winding or confusing. Where they had found no road, God made one and walked them to safety. The detail matters: God's guidance ends not in more wandering but in a settled, safe home.
verses.context: Isaiah 40:3 calls for a straight highway in the desert for God. Proverbs 3:6 promises He will make your paths straight. Hebrews 11:10 speaks of Abraham looking for a city whose builder is God.
explore: Straight path
A direct and level way that leads clearly to its destination.
Led
Guided step by step, the way a shepherd leads a flock to safety.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to make your path straight this season?
verses.alt: A clear trail leading across the desert toward a walled town with palms.

verses.title: Thanks from the wanderers
verses.heading: His wonders to the sons of men
verses.meaning: Verse 8 gives the second refrain: 'Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.' The rescued are called to remember and give thanks. God's acts are called wonders, and they are done for ordinary people, 'the sons of men.' Rescue that is not followed by thanks is rescue half received.
verses.context: Luke 17:15-18 tells of the one healed leper who returned to give thanks. Psalm 103:2 urges, 'Do not forget all His kind deeds.' 1 Thessalonians 5:18 calls believers to give thanks in every circumstance.
explore: Wonders
Amazing acts of God that cause awe and show His power and care.
Sons of men
Human beings in general, ordinary people of every kind.
verses.reflect: What rescue in your life have you not yet thanked God for?
verses.alt: Travelers drinking from a town fountain, faces lifted in thanks.

verses.title: Satisfied and filled
verses.heading: He fills the hungry with good things
verses.meaning: Verse 9 says, 'For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.' This is the reason for thanks. God does not only keep the hungry alive; He fills them with good things. His provision is generous. Mary's song in Luke 1 picks up these very words about God filling the hungry. The verse also explains why the wanderers should thank Him: He gave more than they asked.
verses.context: Luke 1:53 says, 'He has filled the hungry with good things.' Isaiah 55:1-2 invites the thirsty to come and eat what is good. Matthew 5:6 blesses those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.
explore: Satisfies
Meets a need fully, so that the longing is quieted and at rest.
Good things
Generous gifts, more than bare survival, that show God's kindness.
verses.reflect: Where are you looking for satisfaction apart from God?
verses.alt: A table of bread, fruit and water set before weary travelers.

verses.title: Prisoners in darkness
verses.heading: In affliction and chains
verses.meaning: Verse 10 begins the second scene: 'Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and chains.' These people are not lost but locked up. They sit in deep darkness, bound and suffering. Darkness and chains are pictures of every kind of bondage, from literal prison to the grip of despair.
verses.context: Isaiah 42:7 says God's servant will open blind eyes and free captives from darkness. Luke 1:79 speaks of light for those in darkness and the shadow of death. Lamentations 3:6-7 describes being walled in and weighed down with chains.
explore: Shadow of death
Deep darkness, a place that feels close to death itself.
Affliction
Suffering and hardship that wears a person down over time.
verses.reflect: What feels like a dark prison in your life right now?
verses.alt: A dim stone cell with a single shaft of light on a seated prisoner.

verses.title: Why they were bound
verses.heading: They rebelled against God's words
verses.meaning: Verse 11 explains: 'because they rebelled against the words of God and despised the counsel of the Most High.' Unlike the wanderers, these prisoners brought their trouble on themselves. They rejected God's word. The psalm is honest about the cause, yet the rescue that follows shows God's mercy reaches even those whose chains are self-made.
verses.context: 2 Chronicles 36:15-16 says Judah mocked God's messengers until there was no remedy. Proverbs 1:24-31 warns that rejecting wisdom brings its own consequences. Isaiah 5:24 says they despised the word of the Holy One.
explore: Rebelled
Resisted and turned against authority, refusing to obey.
Most High
A title for God emphasizing that He is above every power and ruler.
verses.reflect: Are there chains in your life that came from ignoring God's word?
verses.alt: An open scroll lying ignored on a dusty floor.

verses.title: Humbled by labor
verses.heading: No one to help
verses.meaning: Verse 12 says, 'He humbled their hearts with hard labor; they stumbled, and there was no one to help.' Their suffering humbled them. Hard work wore them down until they fell, and no one came. The verse shows that God sometimes uses hardship to bring proud hearts low so they will finally look to Him. No human helper appeared, which left them with nowhere to turn but God.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 8:2-3 says God humbled Israel in the wilderness to teach them. Psalm 119:71 says, 'It was good for me to be afflicted.' Isaiah 63:5 speaks of looking and finding no one to help.
explore: Humbled
Brought low, so that pride gives way to dependence.
Stumbled
Tripped and fell under a weight too heavy to carry.
verses.reflect: How has a hard season humbled you and turned you toward God?
verses.alt: A worker collapsed beside a pile of quarry stones.

verses.title: The prisoners cry out
verses.heading: He saved them from their distress
verses.meaning: Verse 13 repeats the refrain: 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress.' The prisoners' rebellion did not stop God from hearing them. Even those who caused their own suffering can cry out, and God responds. The same rescue offered to the lost is offered to the guilty.
verses.context: 2 Chronicles 33:12-13 tells of Manasseh, imprisoned for his sin, humbling himself and being restored. Jonah 2:2 records Jonah calling from the belly of the fish. 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness to those who confess.
explore: Saved
Rescued from danger or harm and brought into safety.
Trouble
A narrow, tight place where a person is pressed and cannot escape.
verses.reflect: Do you believe God will hear you even when your trouble is your fault?
verses.alt: A prisoner kneeling in a cell, hands folded in prayer.

verses.title: Chains broken
verses.heading: Brought out of darkness
verses.meaning: Verse 14 says, 'He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke away their chains.' God reversed every part of their prison. Darkness gave way to light, death's shadow to life, and chains were snapped. Freedom is not partial; God brings them all the way out. The words answer verse 10 point by point, undoing each part of their captivity.
verses.context: Acts 12:6-10 tells of Peter's chains falling off and the gate opening. Isaiah 61:1 promises freedom for captives. Psalm 116:16 says, 'You have broken my bonds.'
explore: Brought out
Led from inside to outside, from confinement into open freedom.
Broke away
Snapped and removed, so that nothing binding remains.
verses.reflect: What chain do you need God to break in your life today?
verses.alt: Broken iron shackles lying in a bright prison doorway.

verses.title: Thanks from the freed
verses.heading: Loving devotion to the prisoners
verses.meaning: Verse 15 repeats the call: 'Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.' Those set free are invited to give thanks. Their freedom is a wonder of God's loyal love. Former prisoners have a particular kind of thankfulness, because they know what they were saved from.
verses.context: Luke 7:47 says one who is forgiven much loves much. Psalm 126:1-3 describes the joy of captives restored. Colossians 1:13-14 thanks God for rescuing us from darkness.
explore: Loving devotion
God's loyal covenant love, which keeps faith with His people even in their failures.
Give thanks
To acknowledge with gratitude what has been received from another.
verses.reflect: How has receiving God's mercy made you more thankful toward Him?
verses.alt: A freed man embracing family outside a prison gate.

verses.title: Bronze and iron broken
verses.heading: Gates and bars cut through
verses.meaning: Verse 16 explains why: 'For He has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron.' No prison is too strong for God. Bronze gates and iron bars were the strongest security in the ancient world. God breaks through them as easily as a person opens a door. The verse may also recall the return from Babylon, when God opened the way home for captives.
verses.context: Isaiah 45:2 promises God will break down bronze gates and cut through iron bars for Cyrus. Matthew 16:18 says the gates of Hades will not prevail against the church. Revelation 1:18 says Jesus holds the keys of death.
explore: Gates of bronze
Heavy metal doors of fortresses and prisons, nearly impossible to break.
Bars of iron
Strong bolts that lock gates and cells shut against escape.
verses.reflect: What feels impossible to break through, and how does this verse speak to it?
verses.alt: A massive bronze gate lying broken open in a city wall.

verses.title: Fools in rebellion
verses.heading: They suffered affliction
verses.meaning: Verse 17 begins the third scene: 'Fools, in their rebellious ways, and through their iniquities, suffered affliction.' These are people whose foolish choices brought sickness and suffering. In Scripture a fool is not someone unintelligent but someone who lives as though God does not matter. Their own ways led them into pain.
verses.context: Psalm 14:1 says the fool says in his heart there is no God. Proverbs 13:20 warns that a companion of fools suffers harm. Galatians 6:7-8 says a person reaps what they sow.
explore: Fools
People who ignore God and wisdom, living by their own impulses.
Iniquities
Wrong deeds and twisted ways that turn a life away from God.
verses.reflect: Where might you be living as though God does not matter?
verses.alt: A sick man lying on a mat in a dim room, untouched food nearby.

verses.title: Near death's gates
verses.heading: They loathed all food
verses.meaning: Verse 18 says, 'They loathed all food and drew near to the gates of death.' Their illness was so severe they could not eat. They were close to death's door. The 'gates of death' pictures death as a city they were about to enter. They had come to the very edge. Their own rebellion had brought them here, yet the next verse shows they were not beyond reach.
verses.context: Job 33:19-22 describes a sick person loathing food and drawing near the pit. Psalm 9:13 prays to be lifted from the gates of death. Isaiah 38:10 records Hezekiah thinking he would pass through death's gates.
explore: Loathed
Found disgusting, unable to bear even the thought of eating.
Gates of death
A picture of death as a city, with the dying standing at its entrance.
verses.reflect: Have you ever felt close to the edge, and who did you turn to?
verses.alt: A family keeping watch by a sickbed at night by lamplight.

verses.title: The sick cry out
verses.heading: Saved from their distress again
verses.meaning: Verse 19 repeats the refrain: 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress.' Even those near death can call, and God hears. The repetition is meant to build confidence. The same God who rescued wanderers and prisoners now rescues the sick. Sickness that came from foolishness is still not a closed door to God's mercy.
verses.context: James 5:14-15 tells the sick to call the elders to pray. 2 Kings 20:2-5 records Hezekiah praying and God adding years to his life. Psalm 30:2 says, 'I cried to You for help, and You healed me.'
explore: Cried out
Called urgently for help, here from a sickbed near death.
Saved
Rescued and preserved, brought back from danger to life.
verses.reflect: Who in your life needs you to pray for their healing?
verses.alt: A sick woman whispering a prayer with her hands clasped on her blanket.

verses.title: He sent His word
verses.heading: He healed them
verses.meaning: Verse 20 says, 'He sent forth His word and healed them; He rescued them from the Pit.' God's healing came through His word. He spoke, and it was done. This beautiful line pictures God's word as a messenger sent out to bring life. Christians see in it a picture of Jesus, the Word made flesh, who healed with a word.
verses.context: Matthew 8:8 records the centurion asking Jesus to only say the word. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Isaiah 55:11 says God's word will not return empty.
explore: Sent forth His word
God speaking a command that goes out and accomplishes His will.
The Pit
A name for the grave or death, the place of the dead.
verses.reflect: How has God's word brought healing to your heart or life?
verses.alt: A messenger running down a hillside road toward a village at dawn.

verses.title: Thanks from the healed
verses.heading: Wonders done for the sick
verses.meaning: Verse 21 repeats: 'Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.' Those raised from sickness are called to give thanks. Health restored is a gift of God's loyal love. The refrain reminds healed people not to forget the source of their recovery. The sick who once could not eat are now invited to the table of thanksgiving.
verses.context: Exodus 15:26 calls God 'the LORD who heals you.' Mark 5:19 says Jesus told a healed man to tell how much the Lord had done. Psalm 103:3 praises God who heals all your diseases.
explore: Wonders
Amazing acts of God, here His healing of those near death.
Loving devotion
God's loyal love that moved Him to heal even those who had been foolish.
verses.reflect: What healing, large or small, can you thank God for today?
verses.alt: A recovered man walking outdoors for the first time, sunlight on his face.

verses.title: Sacrifices of thanks
verses.heading: Declare His works with rejoicing
verses.meaning: Verse 22 adds, 'Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing.' Thanks in Israel was not only words but an offering brought to the temple. The thank offering was a shared meal of celebration. Thankfulness takes action and joins words with gifts and joyful telling. Public, joyful telling turns one person's recovery into encouragement for many.
verses.context: Leviticus 7:12-15 describes the thank offering eaten on the same day. Hebrews 13:15 calls praise a sacrifice of lips that confess His name. Psalm 116:17 says, 'I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving.'
explore: Sacrifices of thanksgiving
Offerings brought to God to express gratitude, often shared as a meal.
Declare
To tell openly and clearly so that others hear and understand.
verses.reflect: What could you give or do this week to express thanks to God?
verses.alt: A family carrying bread and a lamb up steps toward a courtyard.

verses.title: Out to sea
verses.heading: Trading on the mighty waters
verses.meaning: Verse 23 begins the fourth scene: 'Others went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters.' These are merchants and sailors doing ordinary work. Israel was not a seafaring people, and the sea often stood for danger and chaos. This scene shows that even those doing their daily business can meet sudden peril.
verses.context: 1 Kings 9:26-28 tells of Solomon's ships sailing for trade. Ezekiel 27 describes the busy sea trade of Tyre. Acts 27 records Paul's voyage and shipwreck on a trading ship.
explore: Conducting trade
Buying and selling goods, here by carrying cargo across the sea.
Mighty waters
The great sea, powerful and dangerous, beyond human control.
verses.reflect: Where in your ordinary work do you most need God's protection?
verses.alt: A wooden cargo ship with a square sail leaving a stone harbor.

verses.title: Wonders in the deep
verses.heading: They saw the works of the LORD
verses.meaning: Verse 24 says, 'They saw the works of the LORD, and His wonders in the deep.' Sailors witness things land dwellers never see: vast waters, powerful creatures, sudden storms. The sea is a classroom of God's power. Those who work in it see His wonders up close. What looks like empty water to a stranger is, to these sailors, a display of the Creator's might.
verses.context: Psalm 104:24-26 praises God for the sea teeming with creatures. Job 38:8-11 says God set the sea's boundaries. Jonah 1:9 calls God the one who made the sea and the dry land.
explore: The deep
The depths of the sea, often a symbol of mystery and great power.
Works of the LORD
What God has made and done, seen in His creation and His acts.
verses.reflect: Where in creation have you seen God's power most clearly?
verses.alt: Dolphins leaping beside a ship's prow on a wide sea.

verses.title: A tempest rises
verses.heading: He spoke and raised the waves
verses.meaning: Verse 25 says, 'For He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea.' The storm does not come by chance. God speaks, and the wind obeys. This is unsettling, but it is also comforting: if God commands the storm, then the storm is not beyond His control. It also means no sailor in that storm was outside of God's sight or care.
verses.context: Jonah 1:4 says the LORD hurled a great wind on the sea. Psalm 148:8 says stormy winds fulfill His word. Mark 4:41 records the disciples asking who this is that even the wind and sea obey.
explore: Tempest
A violent storm with strong winds and very heavy waves.
Spoke
Gave a command; here, God's word stirring up the wind.
verses.reflect: How does it help to know that God is over your storms?
verses.alt: Dark storm clouds and towering waves around a small ship.

verses.title: Up and down
verses.heading: Their courage melted
verses.meaning: Verse 26 says, 'They mounted up to the heavens, then sunk to the depths; their courage melted in their anguish.' The ship climbs huge waves and plunges down. The sailors' bodies and spirits are tossed together. Even brave, experienced men lose heart when the storm is too strong. The psalm captures the physical sickness and the inner terror of a storm at sea in one line.
verses.context: Acts 27:20 says all hope of being saved was abandoned. Jonah 1:5 says the sailors were afraid and cried to their gods. Isaiah 43:2 promises God will be with His people when they pass through the waters.
explore: Mounted up
Rose high into the air, here carried up by giant waves.
Courage melted
Lost all confidence and bravery, as wax melts in heat.
verses.reflect: What situation has made your courage melt, and where did you turn?
verses.alt: Sailors clinging to ropes as their ship tilts on a huge wave.

verses.title: Skill useless
verses.heading: Reeling like drunkards
verses.meaning: Verse 27 says, 'They reeled and staggered like drunkards, and all their skill was useless.' The sailors knew their trade, but the storm was beyond them. They staggered on deck, unable to stand. Human skill has limits, and the storm revealed them. There comes a point when only God can help. Their experience and training could not keep them on their feet, let alone save the ship.
verses.context: Acts 27:18-19 tells of sailors throwing cargo and tackle overboard in desperation. Psalm 33:16-17 says a king is not saved by his army. Proverbs 21:31 says the horse is prepared, but victory belongs to the LORD.
explore: Reeled
Swayed and lurched from side to side, unable to keep balance.
Skill
Learned ability and experience; here, sailors' knowledge of the sea.
verses.reflect: Where have you reached the end of your own ability?
verses.alt: Sailors stumbling across a wet deck, oars and ropes tangled.

verses.title: The sailors cry out
verses.heading: Brought out of their distress
verses.meaning: Verse 28 repeats the refrain once more: 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He brought them out of their distress.' The fourth group joins the others. Out of the storm they call, and God answers. Every kind of person, the lost, the guilty, the sick and the frightened, finds the same God listening.
verses.context: Jonah 1:14 records the sailors crying to the LORD. Matthew 14:30 records Peter crying, 'Lord, save me!' as he sank. Mark 4:38 tells of the disciples waking Jesus in the storm.
explore: Brought them out
Led them out from a dangerous place into lasting safety.
In their trouble
In the middle of distress, not after it has passed.
verses.reflect: What storm do you need to cry out to God about today?
verses.alt: A sailor raising his hands toward the sky in the middle of a storm.

verses.title: A whisper of calm
verses.heading: The waves were hushed
verses.meaning: Verse 29 says, 'He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed.' The same God who raised the storm now stills it. The roar becomes a whisper. The Gospels show Jesus doing exactly this on the Sea of Galilee, revealing Himself as the Lord of the storm. God does not shout the storm down; He brings it to a whisper, a picture of gentle power.
verses.context: Mark 4:39 records Jesus rebuking the wind and saying, 'Silence! Be still!' and it was perfectly calm. Psalm 89:9 says God stills the surging waves. Psalm 65:7 says He stills the roaring of the seas.
explore: Calmed
Made quiet and still, removing the violence of the storm.
Hushed
Silenced, as a crowd falls quiet when told to be still.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God's calm to settle a storm inside you?
verses.alt: A still sea under a clearing sky, a ship floating peacefully.

verses.title: The desired harbor
verses.heading: He guided them home
verses.meaning: Verse 30 says, 'They rejoiced in the silence, and He guided them to the harbor they desired.' The sailors are glad in the quiet and arrive safely where they longed to be. God did not only stop the storm; He brought them to their destination. This is a picture of the final safe arrival God promises His people.
verses.context: John 6:21 says the boat immediately reached the shore after Jesus came aboard. Acts 27:44 tells of everyone reaching land safely. Hebrews 6:19 calls hope an anchor for the soul.
explore: Harbor
A sheltered place where ships are safe from wind and waves.
Desired
Longed for and hoped for, the place one most wants to reach.
verses.reflect: What harbor are you longing for God to bring you to?
verses.alt: A ship gliding into a quiet harbor at dusk, people waving from the pier.

verses.title: Thanks from the sailors
verses.heading: His love on the sea
verses.meaning: Verse 31 repeats the call one last time: 'Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.' The sailors join the wanderers, prisoners and the sick. Four groups, four rescues, four calls to thanks. The repetition invites every reader to find their own story among them.
verses.context: Psalm 118:21 says, 'I will give You thanks, for You have answered me.' Luke 8:39 says Jesus told a healed man to return home and tell what God had done. Psalm 66:16 invites, 'Come and listen, all you who fear God.'
explore: Sons of men
Ordinary human beings, of every kind and background.
Thanks
Gratitude expressed in words and acts toward the one who helped.
verses.reflect: Which of the four scenes in this psalm feels most like your story?
verses.alt: Sailors kneeling on a dock beside their moored ship.

verses.title: Praise in public
verses.heading: In the council of the elders
verses.meaning: Verse 32 adds, 'Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people and praise Him in the council of the elders.' The sailors' thanks should be heard by the whole community and its leaders. Thanksgiving is not only private but public. Telling our story to others builds the faith of the whole people. The leaders who made the town's decisions should hear how God rescued ordinary sailors.
verses.context: Psalm 22:22 says, 'I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly.' Psalm 35:18 promises to give thanks in the great congregation. Hebrews 10:24-25 encourages believers to meet and encourage one another.
explore: Exalt
To lift high in honor, giving God the highest praise.
Council of the elders
The gathering of community leaders who made decisions for the town.
verses.reflect: Where could you share what God has done in front of others?
verses.alt: A sailor speaking before elders seated at a town gate.

verses.title: Rivers into deserts
verses.heading: Springs into thirsty ground
verses.meaning: Verse 33 begins the closing section: 'He turns rivers into deserts, springs of water into thirsty ground.' The psalm now steps back to show how God rules over the land itself. He can dry up the richest places. Prosperity is not guaranteed; it rests in God's hands. The lesson is that the land, like every life, depends on God's continued gift of water.
verses.context: 1 Kings 17:1 records Elijah announcing drought. Isaiah 50:2 says God dries up the sea and makes rivers a desert. Nahum 1:4 says He rebukes the sea and dries up the rivers.
explore: Rivers
Flowing water that brings life and fruitfulness to the land.
Thirsty ground
Dry, cracked soil with no water, unable to grow crops.
verses.reflect: Is there any blessing you are tempted to take for granted?
verses.alt: A dry, cracked riverbed winding through a barren valley.

verses.title: Fields of salt
verses.heading: Because of wickedness
verses.meaning: Verse 34 continues, 'and fruitful land into fields of salt, because of the wickedness of its dwellers.' Rich land can become barren because of the evil of those who live there. Salt land cannot grow crops. The story of Sodom and Gomorrah, once well-watered, stands behind this warning. The verse reminds hearers that a people's sin can bring ruin on their homeland.
verses.context: Genesis 13:10 says the plain of the Jordan was well watered before Sodom's destruction. Deuteronomy 29:23 describes a land of burning salt. Jeremiah 17:6 pictures the one who trusts in man dwelling in a salt land.
explore: Fields of salt
Land so salty that nothing can grow, a picture of barrenness.
Dwellers
The people who live in a place and shape its common life.
verses.reflect: How might the choices of a community affect the land and people around it?
verses.alt: White salt flats stretching to the horizon beneath a hazy sky.

verses.title: Deserts into pools
verses.heading: Dry land into springs
verses.meaning: Verse 35 reverses the picture: 'He turns a desert into pools of water and a dry land into flowing springs.' God can also make barren places fruitful. Where there was nothing, He brings water and life. This hope runs through the prophets, who promised that God would make the wilderness bloom. The God who judges barren places is also the God who loves to bring life where none was.
verses.context: Isaiah 41:18 promises rivers on barren heights and springs in the valleys. Isaiah 35:1-7 pictures the wilderness rejoicing and blossoming. Psalm 114:8 says God turned the rock into a pool.
explore: Pools of water
Standing water gathered in once-dry places, bringing life.
Flowing springs
Water rising from the ground and running freely across the land.
verses.reflect: What dry area of your life do you want God to bring to life?
verses.alt: A desert oasis with clear pools, palms and grazing goats.

verses.title: A city for the hungry
verses.heading: They settle and build
verses.meaning: Verse 36 says, 'He causes the hungry to settle there, that they may establish a city in which to dwell.' This echoes verses 4-7. The hungry wanderers who had no city are now given a place to settle and build. God provides not only water but home and community. What the lost wanderers could not find in verse 4, God now provides for the hungry.
verses.context: Psalm 107:4 described wanderers finding no city. Isaiah 65:21 promises people will build houses and live in them. Jeremiah 29:5 tells exiles to build houses and plant gardens.
explore: Settle
To make a permanent home, putting down roots in a place.
Establish
To found and build up something lasting and secure.
verses.reflect: How is God giving you a place to belong and to put down roots?
verses.alt: Families building stone houses beside a new spring.

verses.title: Fields and vineyards
verses.heading: A fruitful harvest
verses.meaning: Verse 37 says, 'They sow fields and plant vineyards that yield a fruitful harvest.' The once-hungry people now work the land and see it produce. Their labor is blessed. The picture is of ordinary, steady life, sowing and reaping, made possible by God's provision. The work of their hands is real, but the fruitfulness is God's gift.
verses.context: Amos 9:14 promises restored exiles will plant vineyards and drink their wine. Isaiah 65:22 says they will enjoy the work of their hands. Psalm 128:2 says you will eat the fruit of your labor.
explore: Sow
To scatter seed in a field so that crops will grow.
Yield
To produce or give back, as a field gives a harvest.
verses.reflect: What ordinary work could you offer to God this week?
verses.alt: Farmers harvesting grapes in a hillside vineyard at sunset.

verses.title: Multiplied by blessing
verses.heading: Their herds do not diminish
verses.meaning: Verse 38 says, 'He blesses them, and they multiply greatly; He does not let their herds diminish.' Families grow and flocks increase. This is the blessing God first spoke over creation and over Abraham. Growth and fruitfulness come from His hand, not just human effort. Even the herds, the wealth of a farming family, are kept safe by His care.
verses.context: Genesis 1:28 records God blessing humans to be fruitful and multiply. Genesis 12:2 promises Abraham a great nation. Deuteronomy 7:13 promises God will bless their herds and flocks.
explore: Blesses
Gives favor and good gifts that bring life and increase.
Diminish
To become fewer or smaller, losing strength or number.
verses.reflect: Where have you seen God's blessing grow something in your life?
verses.alt: A shepherd counting a large flock of sheep on a green hillside.

verses.title: Decreased and humbled
verses.heading: By oppression, evil and sorrow
verses.meaning: Verse 39 says, 'When they are decreased and humbled by oppression, evil, and sorrow.' Blessing can be followed by hard times. People who once flourished can be brought low by injustice, wrongdoing and grief. The psalm is realistic; life is not a straight line of success. The verse names three causes of decline, oppression, evil and sorrow, without blaming the victims.
verses.context: Job 1:13-21 describes Job losing his wealth and family. Ecclesiastes 3:1-4 speaks of seasons for weeping and mourning. 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 describes being afflicted but not crushed.
explore: Decreased
Made fewer or weaker, losing much of what they once had.
Oppression
Harsh and unjust treatment by those who hold power over others.
verses.reflect: How are you facing a season of loss or sorrow, and with whom?
verses.alt: A family sitting together quietly outside a half-empty barn.

verses.title: Nobles brought low
verses.heading: Wandering in a trackless waste
verses.meaning: Verse 40 says, 'He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.' The powerful who oppress others are humbled. Proud rulers end up like the lost wanderers of verse 4, with no path. God overturns those who misuse their power. Those who made others wander are now made to wander themselves.
verses.context: Job 12:21-24 uses nearly the same words about God humbling rulers. Luke 1:52 says He has brought down rulers from their thrones. Daniel 4:31-33 tells of Nebuchadnezzar driven out to live like an animal.
explore: Contempt
Disgrace and scorn poured out publicly, the opposite of honor.
Trackless wasteland
An empty land without roads, where travelers easily become lost.
verses.reflect: How does it comfort you that God brings proud oppressors low?
verses.alt: A richly robed official walking alone across a barren landscape.

verses.title: The needy lifted
verses.heading: Families like flocks
verses.meaning: Verse 41 says, 'But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks.' While the proud fall, the poor are raised. God sets them in safety and grows their families. This great reversal runs through Scripture, from Hannah's song to Mary's. Families that had been shrunk by oppression are now made to grow again like healthy flocks.
verses.context: 1 Samuel 2:8 says God raises the poor from the dust. Psalm 113:7-9 says He lifts the needy and gives the barren woman a home. Luke 1:52-53 says He exalts the humble.
explore: Needy
People who lack what they need and depend on others to help.
Lifts
Raises up from a low place to a place of safety and honor.
verses.reflect: Who around you is needy, and how might you share in God's lifting work?
verses.alt: A grandmother surrounded by grandchildren in a sunny courtyard.

verses.title: The upright rejoice
verses.heading: Iniquity shuts its mouth
verses.meaning: Verse 42 says, 'The upright see and rejoice, and all iniquity shuts its mouth.' When God acts justly, the righteous are glad and the wicked fall silent. There is nothing left to boast about. God's justice ends the arrogant talk of evil and gives the faithful reason to celebrate. The righteous rejoice not out of spite but because God has set things right.
verses.context: Job 5:16 says the poor have hope and injustice shuts its mouth. Romans 3:19 says every mouth will be silenced before God. Psalm 63:11 says the mouths of liars will be stopped.
explore: Upright
People who live honestly and rightly before God and others.
Shuts its mouth
Falls silent, with nothing more to say and nothing left to boast.
verses.reflect: Where are you waiting for God to silence wrongdoing?
verses.alt: Villagers celebrating in a square while a former bully stands silent.

verses.title: Wise reflection
verses.heading: Consider the loving devotion of the LORD
verses.meaning: Verse 43 ends the psalm: 'Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD.' After all the stories, the reader is told to think carefully. Wisdom is not only knowing facts but paying attention to how God has acted, and seeing His loyal love behind it all. The four rescue stories are given so that we will learn to recognize God's hand in our own lives.
verses.context: Hosea 14:9 ends with a call for the wise to understand God's ways. Proverbs 1:5 says the wise will listen and increase in learning. Lamentations 3:22-23 says the LORD's loving devotion never ceases.
explore: Pay heed
To pay close attention and take to heart, not just hear in passing.
Consider
To think carefully about something and let it shape your life.
verses.reflect: What has this psalm shown you about God's loving devotion?
verses.alt: An old man reading a scroll by lamplight, deep in thought.
